q: Put the stages of a typical ARM embedded Linux boot in order, from power-on to your application.
items: Boot ROM reads the boot pins and loads the first stage into on-chip SRAM
SPL initialises DRAM and loads full U-Boot
U-Boot runs `bootcmd`: loads the FIT image (kernel + DTB + initramfs)
The kernel parses the device tree and probes drivers
The initramfs finds and mounts the real root filesystem
explain: Each stage exists because the one before it can't do the job alone. The **ROM** is fixed in silicon and only has on-chip SRAM, so it can load just a tiny **SPL**. SPL's main job is bringing up **DRAM**, which full U-Boot needs before it can load. **U-Boot** has the drivers to read filesystems and verify the FIT, so it loads the kernel and **DTB** together. The kernel needs the DTB to know what hardware exists. The **initramfs** (if you have one) runs after the kernel and before the real root, and **init/systemd** comes last, as PID 1.

q: A new board revision prints `Starting kernel ...` and then nothing, ever. U-Boot's hash checks passed. What's the **most likely** cause?
options: The kernel is booting, but `console=`/`stdout-path` names the wrong UART, or the DTB is for the old revision
The Boot ROM can't find SPL
explain: `Starting kernel ...` is **U-Boot's last line**, so everything up to the handoff worked. If DRAM were broken, U-Boot (which runs *from* DRAM) would never have got this far. A missing SPL means a completely silent board. A failing systemd unit happens much later and prints plenty of kernel log first. Silence right after the handoff almost always means the kernel can't talk to you: a wrong `console=` or `stdout-path`, or a missing serial driver. Or it means the kernel crashed very early because the **DTB doesn't match the board**, or a load address clobbered the DTB. Add `earlycon` to bootargs to see the earliest output.

q: You're cutting boot time on a camera product from 9 s towards 2 s. Which changes actually help?
options: Set `bootdelay=0` and lock the U-Boot environment
Build the drivers needed for the camera path into the kernel instead of as modules loaded by udev
Add more systemd units so things start in parallel
Start the camera service early, with minimal dependencies, before networking and logging
Use Falcon mode: SPL loads the kernel directly and skips full U-Boot
explain: A default `bootdelay` of 2–3 s is free time to win back. Built-in drivers avoid waiting for udev to find and load modules. Ordering the critical service first is how real head units meet the 2 s rule, and Falcon mode removes an entire boot stage. Simply **adding units** doesn't make anything faster: every unit costs time to start and adds dependencies. What helps is *removing* units, or reordering the critical path.

q: Your secure-boot chain verifies SPL, U-Boot and a signed FIT. A pentester still boots their own kernel in 30 seconds. How?
options: They interrupted autoboot on the serial console and changed `bootcmd`/`bootargs` (for example `init=/bin/sh`), or loaded an unsigned image
The Boot ROM doesn't check signatures
Secure boot only protects the rootfs
explain: A chain of trust is only as strong as its **weakest link**, and an interactive U-Boot shell is a huge one. Nobody breaks RSA. ROM verification is the root of the chain, and it worked. The rootfs is actually the stage that's often *not* protected without dm-verity. Production builds disable the console or require a password, use a compiled-in, read-only environment, require signed FIT configurations (`required` key in U-Boot's DTB), and keep `bootargs` inside the signed config.
